reasoning: All substantive security analysis from the models found no malicious code. The PKGBUILD follows standard AUR patterns: fetching from the package's own declared upstream GitHub repository, using curl/jq in pkgver() to query the GitHub API for version metadata (not executing fetched code), and sha512sums=('SKIP') which is normal for VCS-based packages with mutable sources. No injection patterns detected: no execution of fetched content, no fetching from unrelated hosts. The only disagreement stems from tool errors (HTTP 400, parse failures), not security findings.
disagreement_analysis: Disagreement caused by tool errors, not substantive security concerns. Report 1 (qwen3-235b) failed to audit .nvchecker.toml due to HTTP 400 error. Report 3 (openrouter/free, advisory only) failed to parse LICENSE response. Report 2 (deepseek-v4-flash) successfully reviewed all files and found them safe. The inconclusive verdicts are artifacts of API failures, not security analysis.
coverage_issues: Report 1 (qwen3-235b): .nvchecker.toml not reviewed due to HTTP 400 API error
Report 3 (openrouter/free): LICENSE file audit failed with parse error (advisory report only)
learnings: Tool errors (HTTP 400, parse failures) cause false inconclusive verdicts; implement retry logic or fallback models for API failures
Models correctly identify standard AUR patterns (SKIP checksums for VCS packages, curl in pkgver for version metadata) as non-malicious when properly explained
Advisory reports with tool errors should be clearly distinguished from substantive security findings to avoid confusion in verdict aggregation
The threat model guidance about packaging hygiene vs injection patterns is critical: SKIP checksums for VCS sources and fetching from declared upstream are normal patterns, not security issues
